summary:
Mars Maps is an interactive 3D map of the whole of Mars, built for the people who will one day walk on it. Anywhere on the planet you can plot a route between two points and compare the fastest path with the one that costs the least energy, read the elevation and slope of the ground along the way, and switch between satellite, elevation, thermal and geology layers. Then you can drop to the surface and stand there at eye height, under the Sun's true position for any date.

Jezero crater, where NASA's Perseverance rover drives, is where the map goes deepest. It is one of the best-surveyed places on Mars, with terrain measured down to one metre and a detailed geologic map. There, Mars Maps plans a complete surface walk, a "Marswalk": you choose a landing site and set limits on slope, samples, energy and time, and the app proposes three science walks, checks each against those limits and shows the rover's own photos along the way.

Every number carries its origin: official, derived, simulated or unavailable. What nobody has measured is shown as unknown, never as a guess, because a planner on Mars has to know which numbers to trust.

https://marsmaps.space/ - link

What Mars Maps does

Mars Maps is a map of all of Mars that you can plan on. Across the whole planet it finds routes, reads the terrain and lets you stand on the surface. At Jezero crater, where the data is richest, it goes further and answers a harder question: if a crew landed here tomorrow, where should they walk, and what would they find on the way?

The opening screen. Jezero crater is marked on the globe; every value on the left carries a mark that opens its source.

The Jezero walk planner works in three layers.

1. Plan the walk.

You click the map to choose a landing site. The map is coloured green, yellow or red by how favorable the ground is for landing, calculated from the elevation model and wether the landing site is inside the crater of interest. You then set four physical limits with sliders: maximum slope, number of samples to collect, walking energy and duration. Mars Maps proposes three walks with different science goals:

- Flat bedrock - Exploring the mineral composition of the crater base helps identify materials deposited or transformed during and after the impact. It can reveal evidence of ancient water activity, sedimentation and potentially habitable environments that may have preserved signs of past microbial life.

- Rim to floor - Tracking mineral changes from the crater rim to its base reveals how geological composition varies across different depths and impact zones. This helps scientists reconstruct the crater's formation, understand the redistribution of subsurface materials and identify evidence of past geological processes, particularly water activity.

- Rover check visits places Perseverance has been, to compare with what the rover saw.

Landing colours over Jezero: green is flat ground inside the crater, yellow is moderate, red is steep. The pink line is Perseverance's real path.

The four mission limits. Each default says where it comes from: 20° is a lunar spacewalk figure, the others are project choices. The point panel on the left shows the ground at the landing site.

Three walks planned on the live app on 14 November 2026 from 18.445°N 77.451°E, with the default limits. "Rim to floor" is flagged in red: it is 1.2° over the slope limit.

-

2. Explore the ground.

Use various tools to best understand the path and potential threats.

- Terrain Profile tool - shows the elevation across the path in both 2D and 3D sectors.

2D version provides a graph of vertical position with horizontal distance across two points. This tool is included by default into navigation mode for higher convinience

3D version in the same manner provides the terrain profile but across 3 axis. If the navigation mode is on, it layers the path onto this ground profile so users can better interpret the ground.

- Rover Photos - The app reads Perseverance's real traverse from NASA and draws it on the map, with a slider to move through the mission sol by sol. It places the rover's Navcam photos at the walk's stops, so you see the ground as a camera has already seen it. If no rover waypoint is within 250 m of a stop, the app says that no photo can be placed there.

The USGS geology layer with Perseverance's path up to sol 2022, and the layer menu.

Rover photos for the walk's stops, oldest sol first. Credit NASA/JPL-Caltech.

3. Guide the astronaut.

"Stand at the start" puts you on the surface at eye height, on real terrain with orbital imagery on the ground. A walk guide shows the distance and bearing to the next stop and the steepest slope on the way. A stop card shows the rock unit under your feet, the elevation, the slope and the rover photos taken nearby. The Sun is where it really is at the chosen mission time.

The surface view at the walk's start: the walk guide, the stop card with rover photos taken 12 m away, and the walk from above.

-

Everywhere else on Mars.

The rest of the tool works across the whole planet:

- Routes between any two points, searched on the 200 m global elevation model: the fastest route, and the one that costs the least walking energy. The search keeps off ground steeper than the slope limit, and the route's hazards are listed.

- Four official map layers: satellite, elevation, thermal and geology.

- Terrain profiles in 2D along a line and in 3D over an area you outline.

- The surface view ANYWHERE: stand at any point on Mars, on real terrain, under the real sky.

- Search of official Mars place names, distance measuring and your own marked points.

- A mission clock that gives Mars time and the Sun's position for any date.

A route planned far from Jezero: 94 km across Gale crater and over Mount Sharp, on the live app on 14 November 2026. The panel gives distance, walking time and energy, the hazard check and the elevation profile coloured by slope.

The same region on the elevation layer, with the layer menu open. All four layers cover the whole planet.

Outside Jezero the terrain is known at 200 m instead of 1 m, there is no detailed geologic map and no rover has driven there, so the app offers routes and terrain there but plans full science walks only at Jezero.

Our solution is made with the intent of easiest expansion onto the global missions on Mars. Jezzero is just the most concentrated point due to data available.

How it works

The app runs entirely in the browser. It reads official data directly from NASA and USGS servers:

- Elevation comes from three models. Near the rover it uses the 1 m HiRISE and 20 m CTX elevation models that USGS made for the Mars 2020 landing. Everywhere else it uses the 200 m global model that blends NASA's MOLA with ESA's HRSC. The app reads only the parts of each file it needs, so nothing has to be downloaded first.

- Geology comes from the USGS geologic map of Jezero (SIM 3464, 1:75,000). The app asks the map which rock unit lies at each point and where units meet.

- Slope is calculated from the heights with Horn's method, the standard in mapping software.

- Walking time uses Tobler's hiking function, scaled to the 2 km/h suited walking pace in NASA's EVA planning document.

- Walking energy uses Minetti's measured energy cost of walking on slopes.

- Ground temperature is a heat-balance model on NASA TES thermal inertia and albedo maps. We checked it against two rovers: Perseverance's MEDA sensor at Jezero and Curiosity's REMS sensor at Gale. The app shows the estimate with a ±10 K error.

- Mars time and the Sun's position follow NASA's Mars24 algorithm.

The code is built so that data flows one way: adapters read each external format, a small shared model holds the result, the route calculations work on that model, and the 3D view and panels only display it.

Data you can trust

Every value in Mars Maps belongs to one of four classes, and a small mark beside it opens the details:

- Official: straight from an official dataset, with the source named. Example: elevation −2,570 m from the USGS 20 m model.

- Derived: calculated by us, with the method stated. Example: slope 0.2° by Horn's method.

- Simulated: invented for display, and labelled on screen. Example: the globe's spin speed.

- Unavailable: nobody has measured it, so we show no number. Example: the radiation dose at Jezero. Curiosity's measurement at Gale crater is shown beside it as a cited reference only.

The point panel at Gale crater. Elevation is official, slope and distance are derived, the temperature is Curiosity's latest record beside our model estimate with its ±10 °C error, and the radiation dose is shown as unavailable.

We are also clear about limits. A walk's legs are straight lines that flag steep ground and mapped obstacles; they do not go around them. The 20° slope default is a lunar spacewalk figure, because no Mars figure has been published, and the app says so. The landing colours rate slope only and are not a statement that a landing is safe.

Mars Maps in numbers

The data

- 1 m per pixel: the finest elevation model the app reads (HiRISE, Jezero), with a 20 m model around it and a 200 m model for the rest of Mars.

- 1.8 GB: the size of the 1 m elevation file. The browser reads only the rows it needs, so the first view loads without downloading it.

- 1 : 75,000: the scale of the USGS geologic map of Jezero that the walks are planned on.

- 708 Perseverance waypoints were compared with our elevation models. On the 20 m model the median difference is 1.1 m and 95% agree within 7.2 m. On the 1 m model, over the 612 waypoints it covers, the median difference is 0.0 m and 95% agree within 4.2 m. The rover's heights appear to come from the same source as the 1 m model, so that figure shows agreement, not an independent check.

- 1,859 sols of Perseverance ground-temperature records are available in the app.

The temperature model, checked against two rovers

- At Jezero, against Perseverance's MEDA sensor over 109 sols: 7.2 K root-mean-square difference.

- At Gale, against Curiosity's REMS sensor over 236 sols: 9.3 K. Nothing was fitted on Gale, so this is the independent check.

- The app therefore shows every estimate with a ±10 K error.

One real plan (landing at 18.445°N 77.451°E, default limits: 20°, 6 samples, 600 kcal, 4 h)

- Flat bedrock: 3.84 km, 2 h 28 min, 183 kcal, steepest slope 6.3°.

- Rim to floor: 3.95 km, 2 h 34 min, 191 kcal, steepest slope 21.2°, flagged as 1.2° over the limit.

- Rover check: 0.76 km, 53 min, 36 kcal, steepest slope 8.2°.

Benefits

- A crew or a mission planner sees science goals, terrain, time and energy for a walk in one place, before anyone steps outside.

- The rover's photos show what the ground really looks like, which a map alone cannot.

- Students and the public can stand at Jezero and walk where Perseverance drove, using the same data NASA scientists use.

- Because every value names its source, the app can be checked, and it teaches how to read scientific data honestly.

What we hope to achieve

We want Mars Maps to show that planning tools for human exploration can be built on open data today, and that being exact about what is known and unknown makes a tool more useful. The same approach can be extended to other well-mapped sites, such as Gale crater, as more high-resolution data is published.

Tools and technologies

- Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS 4

- 3D: Three.js with React Three Fiber
